It is meant to be used in conjunction with the [store-front](../store-front) app.\\n+\\n+It is a simple REST API that allows you to add an order to a message queue that supports the AMQP 1.0 protocol.\\n+\\n+## Prerequisites\\n+\\n+- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/download/)\\n+- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/)\\n+- [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/install/)\\n+\\n+## Message queue options\\n+\\n+This app can connect to either RabbitMQ or Azure Service Bus using AMQP 1.0. To connect to either of these services, you will need to provide appropriate environment variables for connecting to the message queue.\\n+\\n+### Option 1: RabbitMQ\\n+\\n+To run this against RabbitMQ. A docker-compose file is provided to make this easy. This will run RabbitMQ 4.x with the Management UI. AMQP 1.0 is supported natively in RabbitMQ 4.0 and later without any additional plugins.\\n+\\n+To run the necessary services, clone the repo, open a terminal, and navigate to the `order-service` directory. Then run the following command:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+docker compose up\\n+```\\n+\\n+With the services running, open a new terminal and navigate to the `order-service` directory. Then run the following commands:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+cat << EOF > .env\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_HOSTNAME=localhost\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_PORT=5672\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_USERNAME=username\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_PASSWORD=password\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_NAME=orders\\n+EOF\\n+\\n+# load the environment variables\\n+source .env\\n+```\\n+\\n+### Option 2: Azure Service Bus\\n+\\n+To run this against Azure Service Bus, you will need to create a Service Bus namespace and a queue. You can do this using the Azure CLI.\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+az group create --name <resource-group-name> --location <location>\\n+az servicebus namespace create --name <namespace-name> --resource-group <resource-group-name>\\n+az servicebus queue create --name orders --namespace-name <namespace-name> --resource-group <resource-group-name>\\n+```\\n+\\n+Once you have created the Service Bus namespace and queue, you will need to decide on the authentication method. You can create a shared access policy with the **Send** permission for the queue or use Microsoft Entra Workload Identity for a passwordless experience (this is the recommended approach).\\n+\\n+If you choose to use Managed Identity, you will need to assign the `Azure Service Bus Data Sender` role to the identity that is running the app, which in this case will be your account. You can do this using the Azure CLI.\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+PRINCIPALID=$(az ad signed-in-user show --query objectId -o tsv)\\n+SERVICEBUSBID=$(az servicebus namespace show --name <namespace-name> --resource-group <resource-group-name> --query id -o tsv)\\n+\\n+az role assignment create --role \\\"Azure Service Bus Data Sender\\\" --assignee $PRINCIPALID --scope $SERVICEBUSBID\\n+```\\n+\\n+Next, get the connection information for the Azure Service Bus queue and save the values to environment variables.\\n+\\n+Next, get the hostname for the Azure Service Bus queue.\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+HOSTNAME=$(az servicebus namespace show --name <namespace-name> --resource-group <resource-group-name> --query serviceBusEndpoint -o tsv | sed 's/https:\\\\/\\\\///;s/:443\\\\///')\\n+```\\n+\\n+Finally, save the environment variables to a `.env` file.\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+cat << EOF > .env\\n+USE_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_AUTH=true\\n+AZURE_SERVICEBUS_FULLYQUALIFIEDNAMESPACE=$HOSTNAME\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_NAME=orders\\n+EOF\\n+\\n+# load the environment variables\\n+source .env\\n+```\\n+\\n+If you choose to use a shared access policy, you can create one using the Azure CLI. Otherwise, you can skip this step and proceed to [running the app locally](#running-the-app-locally).\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+az servicebus queue authorization-rule create --name sender --namespace-name <namespace-name> --resource-group <resource-group-name> --queue-name orders --rights Send\\n+```\\n+\\n+Next, get the connection information for the Azure Service Bus queue.\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+HOSTNAME=$(az servicebus namespace show --name <namespace-name> --resource-group <resource-group-name> --query serviceBusEndpoint -o tsv | sed 's/https:\\\\/\\\\///;s/:443\\\\///')\\n+\\n+PASSWORD=$(az servicebus queue authorization-rule keys list --namespace-name <namespace-name> --resource-group <resource-group-name> --queue-name orders --name sender --query primaryKey -o tsv)\\n+```\\n+\\n+Finally, save the environment variables to a `.env` file.\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+cat << EOF > .env\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_HOSTNAME=$HOSTNAME\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_USERNAME=sender\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_PASSWORD=\\\"$PASSWORD\\\"\\n+ORDER_QUEUE_NAME=orders\\n+EOF\\n+\\n+# load the environment variables\\n+source .env\\n+```\\n+\\n+## Running the app locally\\n+\\n+To run the app, run the following command:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+npm install\\n+npm run dev\\n+```\\n+\\n+When the app is running, you should see output similar to the following:\\n+\\n+```text\\n+> order-service@1.0.0 dev\\n+> fastify start -w -l info -P app.js\\n+\\n+[1687920999327] INFO (108877 on yubuntu): Server listening at http://[::1]:3000\\n+[1687920999327] INFO (108877 on yubuntu): Server listening at http://127.0.0.1:3000\\n+```\\n+\\n+## Testing the API\\n+\\n+Using the [`test-order-service.http`](./test-order-service.http) file in the root of the repo, you can test the API. However, you will need to use VS Code and have the [REST Client](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=humao.rest-client) extension installed.\\n+\\n+To view the order messages in RabbitMQ, open a browser and navigate to [http://localhost:15672](http://localhost:15672). Log in with the username and password you provided in the environment variables above. Then click on the **Queues** tab and click on your **orders** queue. After you've submitted a few orders, you should see the messages in the queue.\\n@@ -0,0 +1,29 @@\\n+'use strict'\\n+\\n+const path = require('path')\\n+const AutoLoad = require('@fastify/autoload')\\n+\\n+module.exports = async function (fastify, opts) {\\n+// Place here your custom code!\\n+\\n+  fastify.register(require('@fastify/cors'), {\\n+    origin: '*'\\n+  })\\n+\\n+  // Do not touch the following lines\\n+\\n+  // This loads all plugins defined in plugins\\n+  // those should be support plugins that are reused\\n+  // through your application\\n+  fastify.register(AutoLoad, {\\n+    dir: path.join(__dirname, 'plugins'),\\n+    options: Object.assign({}, opts)\\n+  })\\n+\\n+  // This loads all plugins defined in routes\\n+  // define your routes in one of these\\n+  fastify.register(AutoLoad, {\\n+    dir: path.join(__dirname, 'routes'),\\n+    options: Object.assign({}, opts)\\n+  })\\n+}\\n@@ -0,0 +1,22 @@\\n+version: \\\"3.7\\\"\\n+services:\\n+  rabbitmq:\\n+    image: rabbitmq:4.3.2-management-alpine\\n+    container_name: rabbitmq\\n+    restart: always\\n+    environment:\\n+      - It is meant to be used in conjunction with the [store-front](../store-front) and [store-admin](../store-admin/) apps.\\n+\\n+This app is a simple REST API that allows you to get a list of products, get a single product, update a product, and add a product.\\n+\\n+Products are loaded into memory and not persisted. So if the app is restarted, the products will be reloaded.\\n+\\n+## Running the app locally\\n+\\n+The app does not rely on any other services, so you can run it locally without any other services running.\\n+\\n+### Prerequisites\\n+\\n+- [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install)\\n+\\n+### Running the app\\n+\\n+To run the app, clone the repo, open a terminal, and navigate to the `product-service` directory.\\n+\\n+If you are testing the proxy for ai-service, you will need to run the ai-service container then set the `AI_SERVICE_URL` environment variable to the URL of the ai-service.\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+export AI_SERVICE_URL=http://ai-service:5001/\\n+export AI_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECS=300 # optional; default is 300s for image-generation proxy calls\\n+export PRODUCT_MAX_SIZE_BYTES=10485760 # optional; default is 10 MB for product create/update payloads\\n+docker compose up\\n+```\\n+\\n+Then run the following command:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+cargo run\\n+```\\n+\\n+When the app is running, you should see output similar to the following:\\n+\\n+```text\\n+    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.16s\\n+     Running `target/debug/product-service`\\n+Listening on http://0.0.0.0:3002\\n+[2023-06-28T02:44:47Z INFO  actix_server::builder] starting 16 workers\\n+[2023-06-28T02:44:47Z INFO  actix_server::server] Actix runtime found; starting in Actix runtime\\n+```\\n+\\n+Using the [`test-product-service.http`](./test-product-service.http) file in the root of the repo, you can test the API. It is meant to be used in conjunction with the [product-service](../product-service/) and [makeline-service](../makeline-service). If you have access to OpenAI or Azure OpenAI API keys, you can also deploy the [ai-service](../ai-service) to help you generate product descriptions. You should also run the [virtual-customer](../virtual-customer) to simulate customers placing orders to have some order data to work with.\\n+\\n+## Running the app locally\\n+\\n+### Prerequisites\\n+\\n+- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/download/)\\n+- [Vue CLI Service](https://cli.vuejs.org/guide/cli-service.html)\\n+- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/)\\n+- [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/install/)\\n+- [OpenAI API Key](https://beta.openai.com/docs/developer-quickstart/your-api-keys)\\n+- [Azure OpenAI API Key](https://azure.microsoft.com/products/cognitive-services/openai-service/)\\n+\\n+### Running the app\\n+\\n+The app relies on the [product-service](../product-service), [makeline-service](../order-service), and optionally the [ai-service](../ai-service) along with DocumentDB and RabbitMQ instances running. A docker-compose file is provided to make this easy.\\n+\\n+To run the necessary services, clone the repo, open a terminal, and navigate to the `store-admin` directory.\\n+\\n+If you have access to OpenAI or Azure OpenAI, open the `docker-compose.yml` file, uncomment the `ai-services` block, and add your OpenAI or Azure OpenAI credentials.\\n+\\n+> IMPORTANT: When filling in the values, do not put the value in double-quotes.\\n+\\n+```yaml\\n+environment:\\n+  - USE_AZURE_OPENAI=True # set to False if you are not using Azure OpenAI\\n+  - AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT_NAME= # required if using Azure OpenAI\\n+  - AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT= # required if using Azure OpenAI\\n+  - AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY= # required if using Azure OpenAI key auth (not needed with workload identity)\\n+  - AZURE_OPENAI_IMAGE_DEPLOYMENT_NAME=gpt-image-2 # required for image generation\\n+  - AZURE_OPENAI_IMAGE_API_VERSION=2025-04-01-preview # required for gpt-image-2\\n+  - AZURE_OPENAI_IMAGE_ENDPOINT= # optional override; defaults to AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT\\n+  - OPENAI_API_KEY= # required if using OpenAI (or as fallback for Azure key auth)\\n+  - OPENAI_ORG_ID= # required if using OpenAI\\n+```\\n+\\n+Then run the following command:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+docker compose up\\n+```\\n+\\n+With the services running, open a new terminal and navigate to the `store-admin` directory. Then run the following commands:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+export VITE_PRODUCT_SERVICE_URL=http://localhost:3002/\\n+export VITE_MAKELINE_SERVICE_URL=http://localhost:3001/\\n+\\n+npm install\\n+npm run dev\\n+```\\n+\\n+When the app is running, you should see output similar to the following:\\n+\\n+```text\\n+  App running at:\\n+  - Local:   http://localhost:8081/\\n+  - Network: http://192.168.0.144:8081/\\n+\\n+  Note that the development build is not optimized.\\n+  To create a production build, run npm run build.\\n+```\\n+\\n+Open a browser and navigate to `http://localhost:8081/`. It is meant to be used in conjunction with the [order-service](../makeline-service) to simulate customers submitting orders over a period of time.\\n+\\n+## Running the app locally\\n+\\n+### Prerequisites\\n+\\n+- [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install)\\n+- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/)\\n+- [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/install/)\\n+\\n+### Running the app\\n+\\n+This app relies on the [order-service](../order-service) and the rabbitmq instance running. A docker-compose file is provided to make this easy. \\n+\\n+To run the necessary services, clone the repo, open a terminal, and navigate to the `virtual-customer` directory. Then run the following command:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+docker compose up\\n+```\\n+\\n+With the services running, open a new terminal and navigate to the `virtual-customer` directory. Then run the following command:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+export ORDER_SERVICE_URL=http://localhost:3000/\\n+export ORDERS_PER_HOUR=3600\\n+cargo run\\n+```\\n+\\n+The `ORDER_SERVICE_URL` environment variable is used to tell the virtual customer where to send the order messages. The `ORDERS_PER_HOUR` environment variable is used to tell the virtual customer how many orders to send per hour. We'll set it to `3600`, which is one order per second.\\n+\\n+When the app is running, you should see output similar to the following:\\n+\\n+```text\\n+Orders to submit per hour: 3600\\n+Order submission interval: 1 seconds\\n+Sleep duration between orders: 1s\\n+Order 1 sent at 14.10ms with status of 201 Created. {\\\"customerId\\\":\\\"1358326708\\\",\\\"items\\\":[{\\\"productId\\\":4,\\\"quantity\\\":3,\\\"price\\\":67.659355},{\\\"productId\\\":9,\\\"quantity\\\":2,\\\"price\\\":21.281868},{\\\"productId\\\":9,\\\"quantity\\\":1,\\\"price\\\":51.21942}]}\\n+Order 2 sent at 1.03s with status of 201 Created. {\\\"customerId\\\":\\\"1888758279\\\",\\\"items\\\":[{\\\"productId\\\":8,\\\"quantity\\\":4,\\\"price\\\":56.293404},{\\\"productId\\\":7,\\\"quantity\\\":4,\\\"price\\\":58.618687},{\\\"productId\\\":4,\\\"quantity\\\":2,\\\"price\\\":19.681084}]}\\n+```\\n\\\\ println!(\\\"Failed to submit order: {}\\\", err);\\n+            }\\n+        }\\n+\\n+        thread::sleep(sleep_duration);\\n+    }\\n+}\\n+\\n+#[derive(Serialize, Debug)]\\n+struct Order {\\n+ It is meant to be used in conjunction with the [makeline-service](../makeline-service) to simulate a real-world order processing scenario.\\n+\\n+## Running the app locally\\n+\\n+### Prerequisites\\n+\\n+- [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install)\\n+- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/)\\n+- [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/install/)\\n+\\n+### Running the app\\n+\\n+This app relies on the [makeline-service](../makeline-service) and the DocumentDB instance running. A docker-compose file is provided to make this easy. The docker-compose file will also start the RabbitMQ, DocumentDB, [order-service](../order-service), and [virtual-customer](../virtual-customer) services to simulate incoming orders. \\n+\\n+To run the necessary services, clone the repo, open a terminal, and navigate to the `virtual-worker` directory. Then run the following command:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+docker compose up\\n+```\\n+\\n+With the services running, open a new terminal and navigate to the `virtual-worker` directory. Then run the following command:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+export MAKELINE_SERVICE_URL=http://localhost:3001\\n+export ORDERS_PER_HOUR=3600\\n+cargo run\\n+```\\n+\\n+The `MAKELINE_SERVICE_URL` environment variable is used to tell the virtual worker where to send the order completion messages. The `ORDERS_PER_HOUR` environment variable is used to tell the virtual worker how many orders to complete per hour. We'll set it to `3600`, which is one order per second.\\n+\\n+When the app is running, you should see output similar to the following:\\n+\\n+```text\\n+Orders to process per hour: 3600\\n+Order f64 = (minutes / (orders_per_hour as f64)) * seconds;\\n+        println!(\\n+            \\\"Order processing interval: {} seconds\\\",\\n+            order_processing_interval\\n+        );\\n+\\n+        // time to sleep between orders\\n+        let sleep_duration = Duration::from_secs_f64(order_processing_interval);\\n+        println!(\\\"Sleep duration between orders: {:?}\\\", thread::sleep(sleep_duration);\\n+        }\\n+    } else {\\n+        println!(\\\"Processing orders\\\");\\n+        let orders = get_orders(&client, &order_service_url)?;\\n+        process_orders(&client, orders, &order_service_url)?;\\n+        println!(\\\"Order processing complete\\\");\\n+        std::process::exit(0);\\n+    }\\n+}\\n+\\n+#[derive(Debug, Deserialize, -->\\n+\\n+# AKS Store Demo\\n+\\n+This sample demo app consists of a group of containerized microservices that can be easily deployed into an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster. This is meant to show a realistic scenario using a polyglot architecture, event-driven design, and common open source back-end services (eg - RabbitMQ, DocumentDB). The application also leverages OpenAI-compatible models to generate product descriptions and images. This can be done using either [Azure OpenAI](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/ai-services/openai/overview) or [OpenAI](https://openai.com/).\\n+\\n+This application is inspired by another demo app called [Red Dog](https://github.com/Azure/reddog-code).\\n+\\n+> [!NOTE]\\n+> This is not meant to be an example of perfect code to be used in production, but more about showing a realistic application running in AKS.\\n+\\n+<!--\\n+To walk through a quick deployment of this application, see the [AKS Quickstart](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/learn/quick-kubernetes-deploy-cli).\\n+\\n+To walk through a complete experience where this code is packaged into container images, uploaded to Azure Container Registry, and then run in and AKS cluster, see the [AKS Tutorials](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/tutorial-kubernetes-prepare-app).\\n+\\n+ -->\\n+\\n+## Architecture\\n+\\n+The application has the following services:\\n+\\n+| Service            | Description                                                                          |\\n+| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |\\n+| `makeline-service` | This service handles processing orders from the queue and completing them (Golang)   |\\n+| `order-service`    | This service is used for placing orders (Javascript)                                 |\\n+| `product-service`  | This service is used to perform CRUD operations on products (Rust)                   |\\n+| `store-front`      | Web app for customers to place orders (Vue.js)                                       |\\n+| `store-admin`      | Web app used by store employees to view orders in queue and manage products (Vue.js) |\\n+| `virtual-customer` | Simulates order creation on a scheduled basis (Rust)                                 |\\n+| `virtual-worker`   | Simulates order completion on a scheduled basis (Rust)                               |\\n+| `ai-service`       | Optional service for adding generative text and graphics creation (Python)           |\\n+| `documentdb`       | DocumentDB instance for persisted data                                               |\\n+| `rabbitmq`         | RabbitMQ for an order queue                                                          |\\n+\\n+![Logical Application Architecture Diagram](assets/demo-arch-with-openai.png)\\n+\\n+## Run the app on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)\\n+\\n+To learn how to deploy this app on AKS, see [Quickstart: Deploy an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster using Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/learn/quick-kubernetes-deploy-cli).\\n+\\n+> [!NOTE]\\n+> The above article shows a simplified version of the store app with some services removed. For the full application, you can use the `aks-store-all-in-one.yaml` file in this repo.\\n+\\n+## Run on any Kubernetes\\n+\\n+This application uses public images stored in GitHub Container Registry and Microsoft Container Registry (MCR). Once your Kubernetes cluster of choice is setup, you can deploy the full app with the below commands.\\n+\\n+This deployment deploys everything except the `ai-service` that integrates OpenAI. If you want to try integrating the OpenAI component, take a look at this article: [Deploy an application that uses OpenAI on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/open-ai-quickstart?tabs=aoai).\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+kubectl create ns pets\\n+\\n+kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Azure-Samples/aks-store-demo/main/aks-store-all-in-one.yaml -n pets\\n+```\\n+\\n+## Run the app locally\\n+\\n+The application is designed to be [run in an AKS cluster](#run-the-app-on-azure-kubernetes-service-aks), but can also be run locally using Docker Compose.\\n+\\n+> [!TIP]\\n+> You must have [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop) installed to run this app locally. If you do not have it installed locally, you can try opening this repo in a [GitHub Codespace instead](#run-the-app-with-github-codespaces)\\n+\\n+To run this app locally:\\n+\\n+Clone the repo to your development computer and navigate to the directory:\\n+\\n+```console\\n+git clone https://github.com/Azure-Samples/aks-store-demo.git\\n+cd aks-store-demo\\n+```\\n+\\n+Configure your Azure OpenAI or OpenAI API keys in [`docker-compose.yml`](./docker-compose.yml) using the environment variables in the `ai-service` section:\\n+\\n+```yaml\\n+  ai-service:\\n+    build: src/ai-service\\n+    container_name: 'ai-service'\\n+    ...\\n+    environment:\\n+      - USE_AZURE_OPENAI=True # set to False if you are not using Azure OpenAI\\n+      - AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT_NAME= # required if using Azure OpenAI\\n+      - AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT= # required if using Azure OpenAI\\n+      - AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY= # required if using Azure OpenAI key auth (not needed with workload identity)\\n+      - AZURE_OPENAI_IMAGE_DEPLOYMENT_NAME= # required for image generation\\n+      - AZURE_OPENAI_IMAGE_API_VERSION=2025-04-01-preview # required for gpt-image-2\\n+      - AZURE_OPENAI_IMAGE_ENDPOINT= # optional override; defaults to AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT\\n+      - OPENAI_API_KEY= # required if using OpenAI (or as fallback for Azure key auth)\\n+      - OPENAI_ORG_ID= # required if using OpenAI\\n+    ...\\n+```\\n+\\n+Alternatively, if you do not have access to Azure OpenAI or OpenAI API keys, you can run the app without the `ai-service` by commenting out the `ai-service` section in [`docker-compose.yml`](./docker-compose.yml). For example:\\n+\\n+```yaml\\n+#  ai-service:\\n+#    build: src/ai-service\\n+#    container_name: 'ai-service'\\n+...\\n+#    networks:\\n+#      - backend_services\\n+```\\n+\\n+Start the app using `docker compose`. For example:\\n+\\n+```bash\\n+docker compose up\\n+```\\n+\\n+To stop the app, you can hit the `CTRL+C` key combination in the terminal window where the app is running.\\n+\\n+## Run the app with GitHub Codespaces\\n+\\n+This repo also includes [DevContainer configuration](./.devcontainer/devcontainer.json), so you can open the repo using [GitHub Codespaces](https://docs.github.com/en/codespaces/overview). This will allow you to run the app in a container in the cloud, without having to install Docker on your local machine. When the Codespace is created, you can run the app using the same instructions as above.\\n+\\n+[![Open in GitHub Codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces/badge.svg)](https://github.com/codespaces/new?hide_repo_select=true&ref=main&repo=648726487)\\n+\\n+## Deploy the app to Azure using Azure Developer CLI\\n+\\n+See the [Azure Developer CLI](./docs/azd.md) documentation for instructions on how to quickly deploy the app to Azure.\\n+\\n+## Additional Resources\\n+\\n+- [AKS Restore, rerun positive validation, clean up, and verify a fresh repeat run.\\n\\n### Negative Validation Plan\\n\\nPreferred negative scenario: make RabbitMQ unavailable to the order workflow.\\n\\nRecommended behavior:\\n\\n- Stop or isolate only the Experiment 08 RabbitMQ resource.\\n- Run the native validator against the running baseline.\\n- Expect non-zero exit.\\n- Require the failure message to identify RabbitMQ/order publication or queue connectivity, not a generic page or process failure.\\n- Restore RabbitMQ.\\n- Rerun positive validation successfully.\\n- Ensure no persistent data corruption or broken environment remains.\\n\\nA DocumentDB negative test is acceptable if RabbitMQ failure proves unsafe in implementation, but the alternative must still demonstrate a dependency-specific non-zero failure and clean recovery.\\n\\n### Kubernetes Versus Compose Differences\\n\\nSupporting Kubernetes evidence at the pinned commit shows these notable differences:\\n\\n- Kubernetes uses prebuilt images tagged `2.2.0` for application services, while Compose builds local images from source.\\n- Kubernetes exposes `store-front` and `store-admin` as `LoadBalancer` services on port 80 targeting container ports `8080` and `8081`. Compose binds local host ports directly.\\n- Kubernetes keeps backend services as `ClusterIP`; upstream Compose exposes backend ports to the host.\\n- Kubernetes includes init containers and probes for startup/readiness, especially RabbitMQ waits. Compose uses `depends_on` health checks for some dependencies and default depends-on semantics elsewhere.\\n- Kubernetes sets `FASTIFY_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` for order-service; Compose does not set it explicitly. The Compose image still starts successfully by upstream design and should remain authoritative for local validation.\\n- Kubernetes workload rates are `ORDERS_PER_HOUR=100` for both virtual services; upstream Compose uses `30` for virtual-customer and `20` for virtual-worker.\\n- Kubernetes resources specify CPU and memory requests/limits; Compose does not. Editing files in other directories requires approval. Network access is restricted.\n# Escalation Requests\n\nCommands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted.
